These funds could contribute to the restoration of infrastructure, expansion of access to credit, through local banks, the development of agriculture, and the creation of new opportunities for millions of people living in poverty. According to the UN data, in 2025, 15 million people in Afghanistan faced hunger and 24 million required humanitarian assistance. As we all know, at the beginning of September, More than 2,000 of our Afghan brothers lost their lives as a result of an earthquake. Tragically, due to lack of financial resources and weak infrastructure, timely assistance could not be provided to those affected. We call upon the leaders of Western countries to immediately return these assets for the sake of future of the Afghan people. If you truly want the Afghan people to overcome poverty, hunger, as soon as possible, return them without delay. Only then will your words about human rights and interstate obligations correspond to your actions. Distinguished participants, today's challenges in African countries from conflicts to food insecurity require not sympathy in words, but solidarity in action. Africa is 54 countries with a population of more than 1.5 billion people. It is the second largest continent after Eurasia. Africa possesses enormous reserves of resources, and we are confident that in the near future, Africa's role in the global economy and international politics will multiply several times. Therefore, the continent's colossal natural wealth must serve the accelerated development of Africa itself and the fulfillment of its own interests. The peacekeeping work of the UN must be strengthened. My country began sending its peacekeepers on UN missions at the dawn of its independence in the early 1990s. This once again proves that we sincerely wish to contribute to the cause of strengthening peace and security in the world. The contribution of a state should not be determined by its size, but by the depth of its commitment and sincere desire for peace and solidarity. We support the strengthening of international treaties, including the Treaty on Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. It is important to educate the younger generation to perceive a world without nuclear weapons. It is essential to raise awareness among young people about the devastating consequences of weapons of mass destruction. The International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness initiated by Kyrgyzstan and supported by the UN member states is an excellent platform for implementing this concept. Kyrgyzstan is one of the initiators and the depository of treaty on nuclear weapon-free zones in Central Asia. We have assented to all fundamental international instruments on disarmament and nonproliferation, including the Treaty on Nonproliferation of Nuclear Weapons and the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. In line with the principle of consistency, this year the Kyrgyz Republic made the political decision to sign the Treaty on Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. We firmly believe that our planet must exist without nuclear weapons. This human invention must be used solely for peaceful purposes. Ladies and gentlemen, for sustainable development and regional integration, the countries of Central Asia require equal dialogue and active cooperation. Despite complex historical and geographic factors, Kyrgyzstan has peacefully resolved its border issues with neighboring countries, in particular Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. This process involved lengthy negotiations and at high political levels, expert levels, and was resolved with due respect for the interests of all sides. I can state with confidence that today, the borders between Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are borders of friendship, trade, and cooperation. This experience confirms that peace is possible where there is political will, respect, and dialogue, which enabled us to resolve existing contradictions and embark on a path of creation and development. Kyrgyzstan is ready to share this experience of resolving complex issues with the international community. Let us use the more than $3 trillion that are spent annually on armaments worldwide to improve people's lives, eradicate hunger, protect our environment, and clean the air. After all, there are no borders when it comes to breathing air. We all breathe the same air. Therefore, I call on us to live not in a race for who has the most powerful weapons, but in a competition for whose country has the cleanest nature and air. Dear friends, climate change is a reality we are witnessing today. We face threats of drought, melting glaciers, changes in ecosystems, and loss of biodiversity. Kyrgyzstan, as a mountainous country, is particularly vulnerable to these changes. We are already experiencing the threat of declining water resources and risks to agriculture and biodiversity. Although Kyrgyzstan is landlocked, it actively participates in international environmental initiatives and can play a significant role in supporting agreements aimed at protecting global eco systems. The Kyrgyz Republic consistently advocates for recognition of the interconnection of natural systems from mountains to oceans, which are two poles of a single system. The future of the oceans begin on the mountaintops. In this context, we ratified the agreement on conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity and become, became among the first 60 plus countries to join the agreement. Rivers that sustain marine and coastal ecosystems originate in mountains. Thus, the protection of mountain ecosystems and the sustainable management of the oceans are interconnected. At present, the country is preparing the second Bishkek+25 Summit, scheduled for 2027, as a central platform for states, international organizations, and experts on sustainable development of mountain regions. We invite all of you to take an active part in this event. Dear friends, as former UN General Secretary Dag Hammarskjold once aptly said, the UN was not created to lead humanity to heaven, but to save humanity from hell. Today, these words are more relevant than ever. The organization was born from the horrors of war, but lives on thanks to faith in cooperation, dialogue, and respect. Now, more than ever, it is important to preserve and strengthen this system of multilateralism as a shield against anarchy and unilateral decisions. There is an urgent need to develop fundamentally new international mechanisms that adequately respond to contemporary challenges and threats. Our organization needs to change. This is no longer a choice, but a requirement of time and today's realities. In this context, we support the effort of the Secretary-General to reform the UN under the initiative UN80. It is also time to improve the reform work of the UN Security Council. At present, 15 members of the Security Council effectively decide the fate of all world's states. Questions of war and peace, security and stability depend on whether they can reach a consolidated position. Moreover, the five permanent members of the Security Council can always block any decision. Kyrgyzstan advocates for a necessary measure to improve the UN Security Council in a way that takes into account the interest of majority of states. In this regard, it is important to achieve a compromise on all aspects of Security Council reform as soon as possible. This reform must be based on principles of universality, broad geographical representation, and wide support among UN member states. Kyrgyzstan considers it legitimate and fair to expand the rights of African states to membership in the Security Council and to eliminate historical imbalances. More than 60 member states, including Kyrgyzstan, have never been elected to the Security Council, while some countries have been elected five or six times. We think it's not fair. Distinguished delegates, Kyrgyzstan strives to make its contribution to peace, global security, and sustainable development. In order to draw the attention of the UN and the world to the challenges faced by small states, Kyrgyzstan has put forward its candidacy for non-permanent membership in the UN Security Council for the period 2027-2028. The support of countries that have never been elected to the Security Council will strengthen confidence in equality among members and thereby raise the authority of the organization and reinforce trust in it. We sincerely believe in the principle of justice, and I ask UN member states to support us in the elections in June next year. Every country should have the opportunity to serve as a member of the Council and contribute to the cause of maintaining peace and security. I can confidently say that Kyrgyzstan is among those states with the experience needed to raise meaningful issues in the Security Council. We will firmly uphold international law, justice, the protection of human rights, and support the multilateral system based on mutual respect, balance of interest, and responsibility to future generations. Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, our challenges are shared. and our responses must be united. Our words must match our deeds. We cannot afford inaction. Peace requires effort. The future of our planet is in our shared responsibility. Thank you very much for your attention.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Kyrgyz Republic. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Gustavo Petro Urego, President of the Republic of Colombia. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

President of the General Assembly, this is my last statement as President here, the fourth time. In my first speech, I announced that it was very likely that there would be conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza and in Palestine and that I suggested that there be a peace conference. But those who don't have bombs or large budgets are not heeded here. Well, four years later, the horrific situation in Palestine did not lead me to think that almost the same thing could happen in the Colombian Caribbean area where unarmed young people are being shot at with missiles in the open seas. And now we are in a different situation. Perhaps it's more global, a kind of Stone Age that has descended on all of humankind, missiles against 17 unarmed young people in the Caribbean Sea, some of them Colombians, the persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion of millions of migrants, missiles that have killed some 70,000 people in Gaza, the lack of action on the climate crisis, All this is linked and all this has the same cause. Migration is simply an excuse so that a rich society, rich, white and racist, believes itself to be the superior race and is not realizing that its leaders are leading it to the abyss, to its own destruction, together with the rest of humanity. They said that the missiles in the Caribbean were used to stop drug trafficking. That is a lie, stated here in this very rostrum. In 2023 and 2024 were years when the largest amount of cocaine was seized. and over 700 drug traffickers were extradited to the United States in Europe. I extradited them. And my government seized, confiscated the cocaine. And we didn't shoot a single missile, nor did we kill any youths. The years where I was able to prove that it's more effective to substitute coca crops, then eradicate them, then forced eradication using poison, enforcing peasants to use it. The violent war against drugs was a failure, and I replaced it with an effective anti-trafficking policy. not based on a mix-up between an inert substance that is drugs with people who actually use it and practice it. But what was necessary is to destroy dialogue and to shoot missiles. Was it really necessary on unarmed, poor, young people in the Caribbean? The anti-drug policy is not meant to stop cocaine that is coming to the United States. The anti-drug policy is to dominate the peoples of the South as a whole. You shouldn't look at the drugs, you should look at who has the power and who dominates. This is why I speak to you as a decertified president. I've been decertified by President Trump without him having any right to do this, a human right or a divine right or any sensible reason. They want to force by violence tens of thousands of peasants to do what the US government wants to do, which are influenced by mafia groups in Colombia. Thousands of peasants are massacred in Colombia. by politicians who were senators, who were presidents, who were ministers, that were bribed and on the payroll of the drug mafia. We must build an international system of accountability that will not hesitate to call evil by its name, regardless of the flag it bears on its shoulder. We must make it clear there are borders, there are human rights, there is international law, and anyone who violates it should face severe consequences. But it is not going to happen by itself, ladies and gentlemen, for the world order is not given once and for all. It depends precisely on us, on the governments, institutions, but most importantly, on societies. As one of the Nobel Peace Prize laureates once said, "Neutrality helps the oppressor always, never the victim." Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented. Let these words be not just a warning, but also a call to action, to action here and now. Thank you for your attention.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Poland. The Assembly will now hear an address by His Excellency Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique. I request for Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Thank you so much. All of this generates unsustainable debt and ever-deepening inequalities in the society. We are witnessing a concerning setback of the international commitments. With only five years to go until 2030, to the agenda of SDG is at risk because the targets have not been met and we still have a long to go. Droughts are turning the population with famine, cyclones into humanitarian disasters, displaces into despair, which is exploited by unscrupulous stakeholders. This is a milestone of universal significance. for countries such as Mozambique, which bears no historical responsibility for the climate crisis, but are amongst those that are the hardest hit by its consequences. droughts, cyclones, floods, inundations. This decision is very important. It's a legal principle for us. It's a call to climate justice. It's a call to global solidarity and immediate actions from the side of all of us. Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but also serious risks of exclusion, manipulation of the society, and even militarization throughout autonomous weapons. These advances pose new challenges to the defense and human dignity, justice, and labor. As long as we do not fully understand how these models work, we cannot entrust them critical tasks without robust safeguards in place. Otherwise, we are going to destroy the world. For that reason, Mozambique advocates a technological and climate diplomacy capable of regulating risk and democratizing benefits. through genuine transfer and sharing of knowledge, of technology, so that the science and technology are not factors of exclusion, but rather instruments of climate justice and inclusive development in the world. Faced with these interconnected challenges, our continent, Africa, can and must play an active role in defining international roles and standards, formulating principles and scientific ethics, and determining research priorities, ensuring that technology innovation is always at the service of the humanity and not the service of destruction of the humanity. In face of this crisis, the isolation is not the answer. Constructive dialogue and strengthening of multilateralism are. The Pact for the Future, adopted in 2024, offers concrete and innovative responses for relaunching of multilateralism adapted to challenges to the 21st century. Mozambique, as an African country with vast natural resources and unparalleled cultural wealth, has distinguished itself in the promotion and strengthening of democracy in the African continent. Since we moved forward with political pluralism, we've been working tirelessly to consolidate the foundation of a robust democratic system, holding regular and transparent elections that reflect the will of people and ensure that every Mozambican citizen has the voice and a say in the decisions that shape the future of our nation in Mozambique. Indeed, our presence in this podium is a result of a free and a transparent process of the Mozambican people from Rovuma to Maputo, from Zumbo to Indico, and in the diaspora. We have historically had an ongoing commitment to dialogue and building bridges between different political and social actors. This commitment to the dialogue was crucial for the lasting peace achieved after decades of conflicts and for the political stability that we enjoy today in Mozambique. Currently, Mozambique stands out for its ongoing efforts to promote an inclusive national dialogue, which the public consultation phase was launched on the 10th September. We are working to ensure that all the sectors of the society, regardless of their origin, political, societal, economic position, they all should be heard and have their concerns taken into account in the national decision. This process will not only strengthen the Mozambican democracy, but also ensure that the country development is truly reflected the needs and aspirations of all Mozambicans without exception. We do believe that the true strength of a nation does not lie only in its ability to resolve conflicts, but also in its ability to promote, in a peaceful and constructive manner, We are proud of the progress we have made so far, and we reaffirm our commitment to continue advancing as an example of democracy in Africa, of peaceful coexistence in the African continent and in the world. We are proud to have promoted during our term the Security Council. where we were non-permanent members, the presidential statement on Africa about the role of Africa in global affairs, as well as to have contributed for the historic resolution 1719, 2023, which paved the way for the predictable and sustainable financing of the operations of support to peace in African Union through United Nation treasure. These milestones confirmed that Africa is not only a beneficiary of multilateral order, but also an indispensable actor in the reforms and revitalization. It is in this sense that Mozambique will keep defending a stronger African voice with two permanent seats on the Security Council and a greater weight in the decision of international financial institutions internationally. A new global financial architecture capable of alleviating debt, mobilizing financial resources for the sustainable development and climate action, as well as correcting historical asymmetries. an inclusive multilateralism, which preserves intergovernmental character of the UN without allowing that this organization can become an assembly of shareholders dominated by the richest. We want to reiterate equally the fact that we want to have two states like Palestine living side by side with peace with Israel as the only fair way, legitimate and long-lasting, so that we can have the aspiration of both people. I would like to congratulate the countries that have recently decided to recognize Palestine, the same right that was given to Israel, contributing to reinforce legitimacy and the fact that we are going to have the solution for both states. The same way, I would like to reaffirm our firm opposition against the coercive measurements that are unilaterally that are excluding the people Cuba to Venezuela, Zimbabwe to other countries in clear violation of the UN Charter against the principles of justice, solidarity, and the international law. Ladies and gentlemen, the topic chosen for this session is like it's better to be together. 80 years and counting for peace, development of human rights could not be more timely. It is intrinsically linked to the events of this week. where we are having this high level in the UN, the celebration of Beijing Conference on Women, the Climate Summit, the first biennial summit for sustainable and inclusive and resilient global economy mandated by the Pact for the Future, the celebration of youth, the elimination of nuclear weapons, and the meeting on global health and well-being. All these meetings reaffirms the vitality and the centrality of the UN and conveys the same truth. What unites us as a humanity is much greater than what divides us. We need today, all of us, to have a renewed faith in the humanity's collective ability to face the common challenges of Gaia, our common home. The world is at a real turning point. We all feel this. Either we deliver the 2030 Agenda that we have written it ourselves, or we will have to accept seeing a relegated and failed promise. And for this, goodwill is not enough. Honoring the principle of common responsibility and differentiality is important. We need resources on a scale. We need to work in a spatter way to align mandate with national priorities for each of us to invest in data. technology, institutional capacity, and most of all, ensure that Africa has a full seat at the table where decisions are taken for its future. The message of Mozambique is very clear. We want partnerships based on mutual respect and shared value. To paraphrase the late president, Samora Machel, the president of the popular Republic of Mozambique at the time, today Republic of Mozambique, international solidarity is not an act of charity, it is an act of unity amongst allies. To conclude, I would like to say that Mozambique counts on the UN and the UN can count on Mozambique. Thank you so much, everyone, and wish you success. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Mozambique. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Luong Cong, State President of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madam President, I would like to extend my heartfelt congratulations to Madam Anna Lena Baierbach on her election as President of the 80th session of the UN General Assembly. I am fully confident that with her experience and able leadership, this session will be a great success. I would also like to pay tribute to Mr. Philemon Young, President of the 79th session, and Secretary General Antonio Guterres for their contributions. Madam President, over the past 80 years, in spite of a multitude of challenges, The UN has stood as the embodiment of humanity's aspiration and collective commitment to peace, cooperation, and development grounded in the universal values of human rights, national independence, equality, democracy, and social progress. Multilateral cooperation has brought forth remarkable achievements, especially in preventing wars. fostering peace and cooperation, building friendships, reducing poverty and curbing diseases, improving living standards, and advancing science and technology at an unprecedented pace. Yet today, we find ourselves in a profoundly changing world facing unprecedented acute challenges. Local wars, conflicts, arms races, and the use of threat of force in the international relations are escalating at an alarming rate. Nontraditional security challenges are exerting heavy tolls on all countries and communities. The global governance, trading, and economic systems are being- are becoming fragmented. and volatile. Multilateralism itself is under strain from strategic rivalry among major powers, unilateralism, and a sharp decline in political will and necessary resources. This is precisely the time to stand united and together promote the irreplaceable role of multilateralism and a rules-based international order with the UN at its heart. Madam President, As a nation that has endured immense pain and losses from wars, Vietnam treasures more than most the priceless values of peace. The spirit of peace, amity, compassion and altruism is deeply woven into our national identity. This forms the bedrock for us to overcome previous sufferings, mend old wounds, shelve the past and look towards the future with the hope to become a friend and reliable partner to all nations around the world. Peace is both the goal and the prerequisite for our journey towards a stable, just, democratic, and prosperous future. Honoring the value of peace and driving robust transformation for a sustainable future is the sincere message that Vietnam wishes to share with the international community on the occasion of the UN's 80th anniversary. In this spirit, allow me to share my reflections as follows. First, honoring the value of peace requires concrete actions rather than just words. We must reaffirm the role and primacy of international law as the cornerstone for peace and equal relations among nations. All countries should clearly demonstrate their responsibility towards upholding international law and the UN Charter and respecting such principles as independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference, non-use or threat of force, and peaceful settlement of disputes. Vietnam welcomes recent efforts to achieve peace and reconciliation which have yielded important results in many regions, such as the peace agreements between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and between Armenia and Azerbaijan. We value and support all diplomatic efforts and hope that they will lead to peaceful solutions to regional and global security issues. We must nurture and practice a culture of peace by building trust, enhancing international cooperation and solidarity, promoting dialogue, listening and understanding, respecting differences, and cultivating friendship among nations. On this occasion, Vietnam calls for ceasefires and an end to all acts of violence, protection of civilians, and facilitation of humanitarian access in conflict zones. Vietnam welcomes the recent recognition of the State of Palestine by more countries and urges the international community to act swiftly to end the humanitarian crisis faced by the Palestinian people. We also reaffirm our solidarity with the state and people of Cuba and call upon the United States to lift its embargoes against Cuba and remove Cuba from the list of state sponsors of terrorism. We must further promote the role of regional organizations in promoting peace, cooperation, and development. International efforts for peace and development will be truly effective when driven by regional organizations in line with the particularities of each region and country. As an active ASEAN member state, Vietnam is proud of ASEAN's growing strength and its centrality in the Asia Pacific's security and development architecture. Most recently, ASEAN contributed to the ceasefire agreement between Cambodia and Thailand, and we are committed to upholding ASEAN's core values of solidarity, consensus, and unity in diversity. building a resilient, inclusive and sustainable ASEAN community, and effectively implementing the five point consensus on Myanmar. we shall also strive to maintain peace, stability, security, safety and freedom of navigation in the South China Sea in accordance with international law, particularly the UNCLOS 1982, while fully implementing the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties and working to finalize the code of conduct in the area. Second, in a world at a historic crossroads, we must transform boldly to shape a sustainable future. Global governance institutions, particularly the UN and international monetary and financial bodies, must undergo vigorous reforms to become more adaptive, ensure equitability, transparency, coherence, and efficiency in their operations, and better respond to the needs of all countries and peoples. Vietnam welcomes and supports efforts to reform the UN, including the UN80 initiative to build an UN 2.0 that is leaner, more coherent, effective and efficient. This initiative must follow a holistic and integrated approach being driven by member states. Vietnam stands ready to share its experience in successfully implementing the Delivering as One initiative of UN organizations in the country. We must build sustainable development models based on digital transformation and green transition, two mutually reinforcing drivers that can spark a sweeping revolution as they stand for convergence. of scientific and technological advancements and environmental sustainability. To optimize this dual transformation, countries must formulate relevant master plans, invest strongly in R&D, train high-quality human resources, and develop green technology infrastructure. Furthermore, it is of great importance to advance international cooperation on technology transfer and mobilization of green finance to ensure that no one is left behind. Developed countries must take responsibility in sharing and transferring technology to developing and underdeveloped countries. In this digital era, societies are undergoing transformation of an precedented pace, scope, and depth, accompanied by rising challenges such as poverty, inequality, unemployment, and a crisis of information and trust. We must ensure that social transformation remains a human-centered process, with focus on such priorities as comprehensively eradicating poverty, providing full and decent employment, and ensuring social justice and inclusion. Vietnam hopes that the second World Summit for Social Development this November will deliver important outcomes and add momentum to the implementation of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. Madam President, from the ruins of wars, once poor, outdated, and isolated, Vietnam has made historic progress. We now enjoy diplomatic relations with 194 countries, strategic and comprehensive partnerships with 38 nations, and membership in over 70 international organizations. Vietnam is now among the world's 32 largest economies and top 20 trading nations. The lives of over 100 million Vietnamese citizens have vastly improved, with a sharp drop in multidimensional poverty rate. We have met the Millennium Development Goals ahead of schedule and are striving to fulfill international commitments and on course toward two strategic centennial goals, becoming a modern, industrialized, upper middle income developing country by 2030, and a developed high income nation by 2045. On behalf of the state and people of Vietnam, I express heartfelt gratitude to the UN and its agencies, member states, and partners who have been walking with us and supported us on this journey of development. Guided by the spirit of self-reliance, resilience, and solidarity for the common cause, Vietnam pursues an independent, self-reliant foreign policy for peace, cooperation, and development while diversifying and multilateralizing our external relations and strive to further expand and deepen our international integration in a more proactive manner, with a strong commitment to being a friend, a reliable partner, and a responsible member of the international community. Vietnam will continue to make every effort and stand with all nations to shoulder our shared responsibilities, overcome challenges, and foster transformative changes to build a world of peace, stability, prosperity, and sustainability, delivering happiness and well-being to all. Vietnam is actively preparing to assume the presidency of the 11th review conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons in 2026. And we look forward to the valuable support of member states for our candidacies to the UN Human Rights Council for the 2026-2028 term and to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea for the 2026-2035 term. We particularly look forward to welcoming you all to Hanoi on the 25th of October for the signing ceremony of the UN Convention against Cybercrime. I thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the State President of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Joao Manuel Gonzalez Lourenco, President of the Republic of Angola. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Switzerland. Your Excellency, the President of the General Assembly, Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, Excellencies, Heads of Delegations, ladies and gentlemen, I stand before Your Excellencies in my capacity as President of the Republic of Angola and current Chairperson of the African Union to speak about my country, to share our perspective on the evolution of the events unfolding in this increasingly troubled world, and to discuss matters concerning Africa, a continent that mobilizes our energies and efforts as we seek solutions to finally a work it once for all towards development. Allow me to extend my congratulations to her Excellency Annalena Baerbock on her election to the distinguished office of the President of the United Nations General Assembly, convinced that her experience and the knowledge she has accumulated through the various functions she has performed with great mastery will ensure the success of the work she has taken on since the beginning of this month of September. I also would like to congratulate her predecessor, His Excellency Philemon Yang, for the assertive manner in which he presided over the General Assembly during the past year, having devoted his utmost dedication to ensuring that this body should operate with commendable efficiency, a fact that rightfully deserves our collective recognition in light of the positive outcomes achieved throughout his tenure. I cannot fail to acknowledge His Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, for the role that he has so ably played with a profound sense of commitment underpinned by his admirable qualities as a man of dialogue and peace amid prevailing geopolitical complexities. Madam President, Excellencies, Eighty years have elapsed since, compelled by imperatives of that era, a group of nations and their respective leaders took the wise decision to establish the United Nations Organization, which from that moment... through both turbulent and peaceful instances, had succeeded in fulfilling its great mission of maintaining the global peace and stability, contributing to the advancement of humanity and to preserve and deepen respect for human rights. This is a great achievement of the peoples of our planet, which cannot and must not be neglected and underestimated by any power, political leaders or by anyone, lest by magnifying egocentric visions and interests, we forfeit the benefits of peace bequeathed to us by women and men who, over time, led us so far in an environment of harmony and global understanding. This journey has not always been linear. Yet, in the most critical moments, prudence has prevailed over the worst impulses of large-scale conflict, and this has been possible solely through continual dialogue, which has proven to be the only factor capable of bridging differences, overcoming obstacles and appeasing even the most troubled and belligerent spirits. Today, these lessons from the past are of great value and must serve as our sole references that guide us toward solution to the conflicts in Africa, Europe, the Middle East, Latin America, in Asia, and wherever they may arise. Under the context of uncertainty in which we celebrate the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, the theme, Better Together, 80 years and beyond for peace, development and human rights, holds a significance that compels us to reflect upon the profound meaning of the appeal by Her Excellency the President of the General Assembly for the renewal of multilateralism and solidarity in action within a framework of collective and complementary undertakings by a more agile, effective and responsible UN as envisaged in the roadmap of the Secretary-General's Initiative 80. In light of these perspectives, it is urgent that we revitalize the United Nations and lift it from the complex situation in which it finds itself currently in order to restore the active role that he has always played, a strongly valuable role that, during the Cold War, gave us assurance of never feeling as close to a global conflict as we do at this moment amid the profound dissonance prevailing in international relations. The main world powers appear to be turning their backs on one another, distancing themselves from even the most basic points of convergence that would allow them to remain committed, above all, to dialogue and concerted action. Today's challenges confront us with a choice, either to do everything in our power to preserve peace or to face war with all its consequences, thus jeopardizing the future of humanity. Those world powers that in the past played a crucial role in the liberation of Europe and its people from the clutches of Nazism and fascism, as well as in the liberation of Africa and its people from the apartheid regime in South Africa, cannot today act differently by aggressing other countries, invading and annexing foreign territories, nor by financing or organizing upheavals that could cause to the overthrow of legitimate governments as we currently witness in our own continent. With this dangerous precedent, no regional, continental or global institution will henceforth have the moral authority to call any state to reason when it breaches the principles that govern the UN Charter and international law. We Africans from countries that endured centuries of colonization perhaps understand better than anyone else the importance of peace, for we have had to face daily struggles to provide our people with food, clean water, healthcare, education, and other fundamental necessities. This experience engenders heightened sensitivity to the harmful impact that insecurity and instability have on the attainment of our goals and developmental projects. This reality is further exacerbated by numerous conflicts and wars afflicting countries and regions across the globe, from which we had hoped to find cooperation and fruitful exchanges, so that together we might overcome our difficulties and contribute with our immense resources and capabilities to global prosperity. It is upon this foundation that the Republic of Angola, has sought to make an honest and genuine contribution to resolving the conflict in the Sahel region, in Sudan, and in Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, regarding which our efforts established a negotiation framework with a peace solution that regrettably did not come to fruition in December 2024 as anticipated, but nonetheless remains a valid platform for further efforts being undertaken with the aim of bringing a definitive end to that conflict. Madam President, Excellencies, that conflict and so many others that we recall are to a large extent the result of passivity of the United Nations member states. who have often revealed themselves to be ineffective in the face of invasion of third-party territories and interference in internal affairs of sovereign countries that occurred over the recent years and have not provoked a firm, resolute and assertive reaction, therefore have become fait accompli that lie at the very center of the major tensions that the world is currently experiencing. The consequences of these are very evident before our eyes in the Middle East, where the systematic failure to comply with the relevant UN Security Council resolution regarding the creation of the State of Palestine has perpetuated a conflict that worsens with each day passing. and appears to have no end in sight in face of this proportionate and violent response and retaliation by Israel, which, while having the right to exist as a state and to demand the release of those still held hostage from the tragic events of October 7th, must not, however, be allowed to pursue in Palestine and particularly in the Gaza Strip, a policy of extermination of a whole people. The Palestinian people, who must not be conflated with Hamas, for there is no peoples and certainly no children who are terrorist, has precisely the same right to an independent sovereign state where they may assert their culture, safeguard for the future and provide predictable and secure prospects for their youth. The concerns surrounding that conflict grew ever more severely in the face of silence hesitations and timid response of the international community, which seems to legitimize the expansion of war to other countries in the region, inexorably corroding the authority of the United Nations. There is nothing more serious than the exclusion of the delegation of Palestine from this forum, where it should directly have the opportunity to make its voice heard as member state in accordance with the terms of the host agreement. The failure to guarantee the presence of the President of the Palestinian Authority at this General Assembly sends a profoundly negative signal as it encourages the continuation of genocide we all are witnessing helplessly and with impunity, which delays the resolution of the issue and complicates the efforts that have been made to bring an end to that intricate conflict. We strongly condemn this unilateral position, which is contrary to the principles that govern the United Nations, even as we urge unconditional lifting of the unjust and prolonged embargo against Cuba, which has dire consequences for the economy and the living conditions of the Cuban people, who struggle daily to withstand a punishment rejected by the international community as a whole. Cuba, which played an important role in the struggle of African peoples leading to the overthrow of the racist and inhuman apartheid regime in South Africa, and by virtue of this was a signatory to the New York Peace Accord of December 22, 1988, which brought freedom to the South African people and led to the independence of Namibia, cannot be arbitrarily and unilaterally considered a state sponsor of terrorism in light of the relevant United Nations resolutions. This model of conduct by a small group of countries, which does not conform to the even minimum acceptable standards of global coexistence, is at the root of the unilateral and subjective sanctions imposed also on Zimbabwe and Venezuela, measures that produce no other results other than the suffering of population who, in an act of great patriotism, adamantly unite themselves in the defense of their nations. Madam President, Excellencies, the authority of this organization, whose foundation is the UN Charter and international law, must be urgently restored without narratives that highlight a logic of double standards. so that just solutions may be sought for the war in Ukraine, or so that solutions proposed by the meeting held in Alaska may be reinforced. Ukraine being a European country, after President Trump met with President Putin on a pragmatic manner and without prejudice to the need for direct negotiation between Russia and Ukraine, one would expect that European leaders, in an interest of Europe's peace and security, would likewise seek direct dialogue not only with President Zelensky, but also with President Putin. We cannot afford to squander this opportunity, for otherwise we risk witnessing an escalation of unpredictable proportions and consequences, not only in Europe, where all active stakeholders must abandon the perilous calculation rooted in the notion of military victory through the weakening of adversaries' capabilities. It is in the light of this the present challenges and the ongoing global crisis that the United Nations must reemerge and become more proactive, lest its role as the main entity for global governance be diminished and be transformed into an institution incapable of ensuring world peace. Therefore, It is our responsibility as states and sovereign nations not to allow the UN to succumb. The United Nations, in its present form,

is the sole organization with capacity to act on behalf of all of us in the quest for worldwide consensus in favor of peace, with the legitimacy to call to reason those member states who undermine its foundational principles in their conduct on the international stage. For this reason, we must preserve it at all cost and adapt it to the realities of the contemporary world through the urgently required reforms. In this most particular regard, I advocate for the reform of the Security Council, in line with common African positions set forth in the Azuwan Consensus and in the Cirta Declaration adopted 20 years ago, which called for two permanent seats and five non-permanent seats for the African continent in an expanded Security Council that is more representative and consistent with the contemporary geopolitical realities. Without this indispensable step, which has already experienced an unjustified delay, we will not be able to ensure the realisation of the Pact for the Future adopted last year, which recognised the urgent need to endow the United Nations with a more democratic and balanced Security Council. This Pact represents a significant opportunity to revitalize multilateralism, rendering it more inclusive and capable of serving as a broader foundation for discussion on critical issues facing today's world. Amongst these, I wish to underscore, alongside many other relevant issues, the issue of financing for development and climate challenge. With regard to matters concerning support for development, there remains much to be discussed, but also it's appropriate to recognize the recent progress achieved with the adoption of the Seville Commitment, reached at the fourth conference on financing for development which advocates the urgent reform of international financial institutions so as to render them more representative, inclusive and equipped to address the pressing needs of the developing countries, especially those of Africa. I am convinced that this instrument, combined with a pact for the future, the Unite Nation Fiscal Convention and the Unite Nation Debt Convention, still under discussion, will together serve as a political, financial and normative platform that will provide significant momentum to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Madam President, Excellencies, it is essential that we confront the climate crisis as the greatest existential threat of our time, which can only be overcome through joint, coordinated and united action. In view of the ongoing increase of global warming and the increasingly violent, frequent natural disasters, it has become imperative that the nations that which derived The greatest benefits from industrial and economic development in the past fully assume today the historical responsibility, ensuring as an act of climate justice, adequate financing, technology transfer and support for adaptation and mitigation for the developing countries. The countries with only residuals share in Greenhouse gas emissions are those that disproportionately and virtually alone face the impact of climate change, global warming, and the devastating effects on agriculture, food security, and public health. In view of such evidence, and the responsibilities arising therefrom. Angola remains steadfastly committed to the Paris Agreement and to implementing adaptation and mitigation measures in an alignment with the United Nations 2030 Agenda and the African Union 2063 Agenda, which each reign The consensus concerning the mobilization of predictable, affordable climate financing intended to ensure a just energy transition capable of protecting the most vulnerable communities. This cross-cutting theme, which demands increasingly heightened sense of responsibility, both within the scope of public agendas and among major industrial corporations will receive due attention at the forthcoming COP30 climate summit to be held shortly in Brazil, which for the second time hosts an event of this magnitude, a testament to the country's commitment and engagement with environmental issues. In 1992, in Rio de Janeiro, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was inaugurated, a paradigm that has proven greatly beneficial with increasingly profound discussion that endured to this day and which will assuredly at the forthcoming conference enable us all to take another step forward on this long journey that we must undertake to achieve the major climate goals aspired by humanity. Excellencies, 80 years after the founding of the United Nations and following the end of the Cold War, our expectation was that we would be living in a world without present uncertainties not as perilous as that which we now witness. Until 1991, we lived in a context marked by sharp division between two ideologically opposed blocs, which nevertheless offered a more predictable framework and was less susceptible to drifting into large-scale confrontation. This flashback should not lead us to the conclusion that the global stability is only possible within a framework of rigid divisions of any kind, rather. It should inspire us to build a system based on balanced interest and shared concern on matters pertaining to global security that fosters complementarity and all forms of convergence within an environment of multilateralism, which remains the sole pathway capable of preserving as from a true catastrophe. With these few words, I thank you for your kind attention.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Angola. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Joseph Nyuma Boakai, President of the Republic of Liberia. I request protocol to escort his excellency and invite him to address the assembly.

Madam President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I am honored to address the 88th session of the United Nations General Assembly on behalf of the people of Liberia. Eight decades after its founding, in which Liberia was involved, our country is proud that the United Nations remains the most critical multilateral platform for international cooperation and collective action. The UN continues to employ the best framework of humanity for peace, justice, security, dignity, and shared prosperity. Madam President, please accept the congratulations from the delegation Liberia on your assumption of the esteemed office of President of the 81st session of the General Assembly. We trust in your leadership to guide the affairs of this august body. We also extend our commendation to your predecessor for his stewardship on the 79th session, and are grateful to the Secretary General for his leadership. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, please accept the gratitude of the Liberian government and the people, the overwhelming trust demonstrated by the General Assembly, members in electing Liberia to serve on a non-permanent seat of the United Nations Security Council for the 2026-2027 term. This marks Liberia's first full turn on the UN Security Council, 80 years after the country signed the charter and helps Theater Auditorium in San Francisco. While the nameplate during this two-year term will read Liberia, the seat, however, belongs to Africa. We are committed to ensuring that Liberia's contribution to the Security Council discussions and the decisions are shaped by hard-earned experiences in conflict resolution as well as our successes in peace building, democratic reform, political transition and governance. Additionally, the collective experience of the continent will be taken into consideration. Liberia looks forward to advocating for Africa's fair representation on the UN Security Council, which can only be achieved through permanent representation as a key part of the UN Security Council reform agenda. Excellencies, when the UN was founded in 1945, nations came together in the belief that peace could only be secured through cooperation. After two world wars, it became a widely held conviction that nations are stronger when united, then when divided. 80 years later, that conviction is being tested like never before. From wars and displacement to terrorism, threats to technological advances, climate change, and widening inequalities, today our world faces challenges that no country can solve alone. At the same time, and paradoxically, when the world needs to strengthen multilateralism, its credibility and efficacy have been questioned. As one of the four African countries to sign the Charter of the United Nations, Liberia feels morally obligated to call for renewal rather than reversal. of multilateralism. Reversal of multilateralism is not an option for a just and peaceful world. We call for greater inclusion, effectiveness, and respect for international law, recognizing that the credibility of the United Nations depends on our ability to act together in the service of humanity. rather than a path in the pursuit of narrow interests. Madam President, wars in Europe, Middle East, and Africa remind us that peace is often fragile and must be constantly defended. Therefore, as in 1945, Liberia once again reaffirms its commitment to the dialogue, diplomacy, and the peaceful resolution of disputes. In this spirit, Liberia supports all credible mediation efforts aimed at resolving conflict between Russia and Ukraine, as well as Israel-Palestinian conflict. Liberia stands on a common African position for the realization of the two-state solution, where Israel and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security in accordance with international law and the relevant UN resolutions. We call on the international community to act together decisively to protect civilians, hold perpetrators of atrocities accountable, and strengthen mediation efforts. Rising from the ruins of civil war, Liberia knows all too well that human cause of conflict and importance of peace. Since 2003, Liberia has experienced three peaceful and orderly democratic transitions, each marked by a smooth transfer of power, making our nation safer, more stable, and more secure after over 30 years of unrest, instability, and destruction. Liberians have also worked hard to achieve this through moderate cooperation, multilateral cooperation, with support from ECOWAS, the African Union, and the United Nations. Excellency, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, for Liberia, Climate change is not a distant threat, but a present reality. Rising seas eroding our coast, wild storms and heavy rain, devastated communities, threaten lives and livelihoods and exacerbate food insecurity. Yet we are acting. We are carrying our coastal defense project, developing climate information system for early warning systems, finalizing our carbon market policies, and advancing the blue economy safety. But our efforts alone are not enough. We urge implementation of the Paris Agreement, full capitalization of the loss and damage fund, and greater global investment in adaptation and mitigation. Above all, we call for climate justice. Those who contribute the least to this crisis should not be forced to suffer the most. Madam President, Excellencies, too many developing nations spend more on debt servicing than on health or education. The current international financial architecture is unresponsive to this reality, making it not only outdated, but also unjust and defiant of the objectives of shared prosperity and development, the pursuit of which the United Nations was created. Liberia, therefore, joins the global south in calling for urgent reform to the international financial architecture to ensure fair representation, a new approach to debt servicing, and financing that supports sustainable development. Shared prosperity requires a system that truly leaves no nation behind. Excellencies, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, at home, inclusive development remains our top priority. To this end, our government have launched the arrest agenda for inclusive development, which focuses on agriculture and food security, roads and infrastructure, rule of law and good governance, education and skill development, sanitation and health, tourism, technology, and innovation. The arrest agenda aligns with our national vision 2030. We aims to transform Liberia into a lower middle income country. And later foundation for a capable state by 2030. Through this agenda, we are committed to improving the livelihoods reducing inequality, and ensuring that every Liberian benefits from the dividends of peace and development. We are taking tangible steps to improve governance by implementing accountability and anti-terrorism corruption measures, such as asset declaration. We are strengthening institutional capacity to promote integrity, transparency, and improve public service delivery. Everywhere has endured some of the darkest chapters of human suffering. Having experienced one of the most brutal conflicts in recent history, over the past two decades, we have remained firmly on a path of recovery, working to heal our nation and rebuild from the painful legacy of war. My government has taken deliberate, meaningful steps toward national reconciliation. These include honoring the memory of the victims, supporting initiatives for memorialization, and upholding the commitment to justice and the rule of law. While we recognize that these efforts are complex and challenging, they are essential steps towards achieving lasting peace and genuine national healing. May I now take the opportunity to renew my government's request for international support and assistance in establishing a war and economic crimes court, which will further the Liberian people's aspiration for national healing and reconciliation through justice. Madam President, for the United Nations to remain relevant and practical, it must adapt. Liberia therefore supports the Pact for the Future and Global Digital Compact. We also call on the UN to be more responsive and reflective of today's world. Using outdated 1945 solutions to tackle 2025 challenges is neither reasonable nor realistic. Regarding sustainable development goals, we agree that our collective progress is too slow. However, reaching the SDG targets remains a vital effort as ever. We therefore urge that the timely achievement of the SDGs be treated as a global emergency. Consequently, Liberia will submit its next voluntary national review in 2026, committing to accelerate the implementation of the global goals in line with the African Union's Agenda 2063 and ECOWAS Vision 2050. Finally, Excellencies, the theme of this session, Better Together, aptly captures both the spirit and the urgency of our time. The challenges before us are immense, so too must be the collective capacity to overcome them. Liberia pledges to remain a bridge to peace, a development partner, and a defender of human rights. For the next 80 years, we will continue to honor the promise of 1945 by renewing our commitment to a world where peace is just, development is inclusion, and dignity is universal. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Liberia. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency, Felix Antoine Tshisekedi Tshisekedi Shilombo, President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madame la Presidente. Madam President, Secretary General, distinguished heads of state and government, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset, I would like to warmly congratulate Annalena Baerbock, on her election as President of the 80th regular session of the General Assembly of the United Nations. Her leadership and her commitment to multilateralism will be crucial for the success of our work. I also here at this podium would like to pay tribute to her predecessor, His Excellency, Mr. Philemon Yeng, whose commitment and dedication were critical to the previous session. Lastly, I reaffirm my country's full trust in the actions of the Secretary-General of the UN, Mr. Antonio Guterres, for his unwavering efforts to strengthen our organization and to promote solutions to the challenges threatening peace, security, and prosperity throughout the world, especially in the region of the Great Lakes of Africa, which includes the DRC. Madam President, I commend the relevance of the theme of this 80th session, "Better Together: 80 Years and More for Peace, Development, and Human Rights." It highlights eight decades of joint efforts of a UN dedicated to peace, development, and universal well-being based upon an unwavering promise of collective security. The 80th anniversary of the United Nations, which is the guarantor of this security and has been since 1945, is an opportunity to reaffirm the virtues of effective multilateralism and to pay tribute to the ideals of peace, human dignity, and solidarity between nations which inspired its founders. Although the United Nations remains a pillar for the regulation of international relations, as well as the prevention and resolution of conflicts and the promotion of human rights and fundamental freedoms, Today, it is facing systemic challenges which are putting its credibility and capacity for action to the test. The profound changes ongoing during our era, especially protracted armed conflict, climate deregulation, recurring humanitarian crises, and constantly evolving transnational threats remind us that multilateralism is not an option, it is a necessity for all of us. We remain convinced that the responses to the challenges of the 21st century can only emerge from collective solutions based upon cooperation, justice, and shared responsibility. Madam President, after its election in June, the DRC is preparing to sit as a non-permanent member on the Security Council for 2026-27. I, on behalf of my country, once again sincerely thank the Member States for the trust and solidarity they've shown toward us. Our participation will be firmly constructive and holistic. it will be based on two indivisible priorities: peace and security on one hand, and prevention and resolution of conflict on the other. We also plan to actively contribute to the development and implementation of a new agenda for peace in order, through our capacity and our experience, to propel reforms of peacekeeping and building operations, as well as the adaptation of the UN collective security system. With regard to Security Council reform, my country reaffirms the common African position as enshrined in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration. Africa must hold two additional seats in the non-permanent member category and two seats in the category of permanent members with the same rights, including veto rights, the same privileges and the same obligations as the current permanent members. With its 54 states and more than 1.2 billion inhabitants, Africa can no longer remain on the sidelines of decisions that concern international peace and international security. Madam President, another priority is the illegal exploitation of natural resources, one of the major and most persistent causes of conflict. The DRC plans to center debate on exemplary governance of strategic minerals in order to guarantee exploitation that complies with the principles of sustainable development, economic sovereignty, and people's well-being on a global scale, breaking the toxic link between profit from mining and financing non-state armed groups requires a comprehensive approach based on harmonizing rules of due diligence and traceability from mines to the consumer, the comprehensive transparency of supply chains and effective beneficiaries, independent mechanisms for oversight and audit, strengthened operational and cooperation between customs, judicial, and financial authorities, targeted and effective sanctions against traffickers and their networks, and a staunch fight against corruption supported by standards of good governance, public contracts, and the traceability of payments. Of course, the dimensions of human rights and transitional justice, as well as the women, peace and security and youth, peace and security agendas remain indispensable to this action. Their effective inclusion is a precondition for a just, lasting and inclusive peace. Madam President. In the run-up to the establishment of the independent commission of inquiry established by the UN Human Rights Council on the massacres perpetrated a few months ago by our assailants and their proxies in the east of my country, I solemnly call upon the international community. It has the moral and political duty to support this crucial body in order to establish truth, bring justice to victims, and lay the groundwork for a lasting peace rooted in memory and shared responsibility. Madam President, as the planet warms, marginalization becomes deeper and conflicts multiply. The diagnosis that in July 2023 inspired the vision for a new agenda for peace by Secretary General remains as relevant as ever. The world is now facing multifaceted and profound crises. The foundations of prevention have been weakened and international law so strongly enshrined in the UN Charter, which calls upon states to refrain from the threat or use of force, is too often flouted. Our system of collective security is being shaken. It will not survive without a massive increase in solidarity of interest and compliance with rules. In this context, the rhetoric of war is gaining ground. And we are helplessly watching the return of old demons, armed aggression, wars over resources, and for the conquest of vital territory, which have spared no continent. While the war between Israel and Hamas is ravaging Gaza with the risk of regional spillover, and the Russian-Ukrainian conflict continues, other hotspots are raging in Yemen, Myanmar, and Syria. The armed conflict that is continuing in my country is a tragic example of this. For three decades now, peace and security have broken down in the east of the DRC. This war has transformed into a predatory enterprise. It has long since transcended merely military or geopolitical dimensions. It aims to pillage our resources, erase our collective memory, and destroy our communities. Its consequences are catastrophic. Millions of deaths, decimated families, almost 7 million IDPs, women and children who've been targeted, villages razed to the ground, generations sacrificed. In several regions of the east, We see all the indicators of an attempt at extermination. The UN itself, through the mapping report, has documented the scale of these atrocities. This is not just a conflict. It is a silent genocide that the Congolese people have been suffering for more than 30 years. In July, more than 300 civilians, including 48 women and 19 children, were massacred in the territory of Rutshuru by the AFC and M23 with the support of the Rwandan Defense Forces. These crimes are not isolated incidents. They are part of a gruesome whole. I thank the United States for taking the initiative last month of convoking an extraordinary session of the Security Council to examine these massacres, which were documented by Human Rights Watch. To end this conflict, the Security Council in Resolution 2773 of February 21, 2025, called for the withdrawal of M23 from the cities of Goma and Bukavu and from all the areas under its control, as well as for the dismantling of the parallel administrations established in violation of the sovereignty of the DRC, as well as an end to all assistance, direct or indirect, to M23. Here, I commend the leadership of President Donald Trump, who paved the way for a dialogue that led to the signing on June 27, 2025 in Washington of a peace agreement between the DRC and Rwanda. This agreement explicitly requires that Kigali carries out a complete and verifiable withdrawal of its troops and lifts so-called defensive measures. It also calls for the disengagement, disarmament, and conditional integration of non-state armed groups within the armed forces of the DRC and the Congolese National Police. the establishment of a joint mechanism of security coordination, as well as a provision guaranteeing respect for territorial integrity and a cessation of hostilities. The withdrawal of Rwandan troops, the end of their support to M23, and the restoration of the authority of the Congolese state over all the occupied areas are non-negotiable conditions for a real peace. I call upon the United Nations to ensure the strict enforcement of this agreement, which is now critical to the implementation of the aforementioned resolution. Until these decisions are carried out, the blood of innocents will continue to flow. In the same vein, the DRC and the AFCM 23 signed on July 19, 2025. in Doha, a declaration of principles that commit the parties to strive together toward a peaceful solution. I would like to thank His Highness the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, for his dedication and commitment to peace in the DRC and in the Great Lakes region. Lastly, I express my deep appreciation for the coordination provided by His Excellency, President of the Council of Ministers of Togo, as part of the Lome process. This dynamic emerges from the convergence of the efforts of the Luanda process, which have been constantly led by His Excellency Joao Manuel Goncalves Lourenco, President of the Republic of Angola and acting President of the African Union, current President of the African Union, as well as the Nairobi process facilitated by His Excellency Uhuru Muigai Kenyatta, former President of the Republic of Kenya. Together, these initiatives have laid the groundwork for a unified mechanism of regional facilitation. This momentum is something we hope to maintain to preserve continental cohesion, strengthen coordination between African initiatives, and establish a harmonized framework for action in order to restore lasting peace to the east of the DRC. Our goal remains unchanged to bring about just, lasting, and verifiable peace. not just an empty and ephemeral period of calm, which almost 30 years now has too often disappointed our people. We expect that the international community to stand on the side of right with constancy and courage. That is how truth will win out over impunity, and that peace will become possible, Madam President. The diplomatic process being carried out with all parties to the conflict is in no way incompatible with justice and reparations. If the world still hesitates to put a name to our pain, well, we will not wait. We are the main witnesses of it. We will be those who bring about justice. But we need your solidarity, your support, as well as complete compliance with international law. The DRC does not need charity or condolences. It needs justice, truth, and dignity. Our country is doing its part. We've signed peace agreements. agreed to dialogue, made commitments toward reconciliation. But a false peace based on impunity and forgetting is only a precarious truce. History will not judge our speeches, but our ability to recognize mass crimes, including genocide, and to end impunity.

Madame la Presidente.

Madam President, The DRC is a country full of life, natural wealth, and human resilience. We want to contribute to global peace, but peace begins with recognition of our own tragedy. I solemnly call upon this Assembly to recognize the Congolese genocide, to support our battle for truth and justice, and to help us, at last, build lasting peace in the heart of Africa. We call upon the UN to establish a regime of targeted sanctions against perpetrators of economic crimes, as well as crimes, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and crimes of genocide that have been committed in the east of my country. We call upon the UN to support all actions that aim to curb illicit supply chains in minerals, which for decades now have been financing war and human tragedy. These actions must be implemented with the support of the African Union, the UN, and our development partners, with the involvement of adjacent states, as well as businesses that purchase and process these minerals stained with blood, as well as financial institutions. through which these cash transits, as well as civil society organizations. I state this solemnly. The international community has the moral and political duty to recognize this tragedy for what it is, a genocide, and to act accordingly. Silence and inaction in the face of these crimes amounts to complicity. We call for the immediate establishment of an international commission of inquiry that is independent and sufficiently funded to establish truth, bring justice to victims, and break the cycle of impunity that has been fueling this tragedy for decades. Madam President, terrorism remains a serious threat to peace and international security. No region of the world has been spared. After Asia, Western Europe, and North America, this scourge has become rooted in Africa and is destabilizing several subregions. Al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb, although eroded by international action, maintains some capacity in gray zones and is spreading its influence. Boko Haram in the north of Nigeria and al-Shabaab in Somalia maintain significant territorial control. In Central Africa, after the devastation caused by the Lord's Resistance Army, or LRA, led by Joseph Kony, the northeast of the DRC is suffering. under the Allied Democratic Forces, a Ugandan terrorist group that has sworn allegiance to the Islamic State. These extremist groups have left behind them. in their wake a devastating toll of loss of human life and continue to threaten regional stability. A member of the Global Coalition against ISIS, the DRC calls on the UN to more staunchly implement the recommendations of this coalition and the ACABA process, that is to say the sharing of intelligence, curbing of financing, combat against propaganda, and sanctuaries for terrorism, as well as increased support to victim communities while fully respecting international humanitarian law. Madam President, as we face a climate crisis, the Paris Agreement remains a crucial legal framework for the accountability of states when it comes to emissions and adaptation to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Thus, the DRC has adopted its National Adaptation Plan 2022-2026. We have committed to stopping and reversing deforestation and forest degradation, land degradation by 2031, while promoting sustainable development and inclusive rural transformation. Since December 2021, A package of measures has supported the restoration of forests, especially the school garden program to plant a billion trees by 2030. This aims to strengthen CO2 sequestration and the resilience of our ecosystems. We commend the adoption of the 5/CMA.5 decision, which establishes new financing mechanisms, including the loss and damages fund to complement existing resources and to provide tangible solutions for the most vulnerable countries. With our unique environmental capacity, the DRC is at the heart of these solutions. It's prepared to mobilize its natural assets to protect the global climate. as long as financial commitments are predictable, accessible, and commensurate with environmental and human imperatives. Madam President, allow me also to address the issue of energy challenges and the protection of our ecosystems. I'd like to recall that the Congo Basin is home to the second largest tropical forest in the world, considered by many scientists to be the largest land-based carbon sink, as well as a vast hydrographic network dominated by the Congo River, the second largest in the world in terms of throughput. These vital resources are severely threatened by destructive activities, including deforestation, illegal exploitation, and pollution, which are often exacerbated by recurring armed conflict. which amount to real crimes against nature. That is why the DRC supports the initiative spearheaded by Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa to establish at the international level ecocide as a crime in order to punish illicit acts and arbitrary actions that cause severe environmental damage. Madam President, the adoption of the Pact for the Future recalls the necessity of accelerating the implementation of the SDGs five years before the deadline of 2030. The DRC has placed this imperative at the center of its action through the Strategic National Development Plan 2024-2028, which places the Congolese people at the heart of its priorities and incorporates the three dimensions of sustainable development, the environmental, social, and economic dimensions. This plan is based on clear guidelines, including strengthening democratic governance and security, modernizing infrastructure and the business environment, protecting the environment, and guaranteeing access to essential social services, including water, sanitation, education, healthcare, electricity, and so forth. The results have been mixed. For only SDGs 12 and 13 still seem attainable by 2030, but concrete progress has been made. Free education has allowed more than 5 million children to return to school. Universal health coverage has expanded access to high quality healthcare. women's empowerment policies are reducing socioeconomic gaps. These accomplishments, however, are jeopardized by the persistent lack of security in the east of the country and the vulnerability of our economy to external shocks. Our economy, therefore, must transform in order to become a driver of sustainability and prosperity. My country is a solution to climate challenges. My country plans to make full use of its forests, its biodiversity within a climate economy that is turned toward a green, resilient. low carbon type of growth. In this regard, the Grand Inga project, one of the largest hydroelectric complexes in the world, embodies our ambition and strengthens the position of the DRC as a country of solutions. It provides clean, competitive energy to provide electricity to our territory, to decarbonize our industries, to support regional energy integration and to pave the way for new applications, including green hydrogen. This trajectory is based on developing integrated carbon markets, attracting responsible investment, and creating decent jobs and sustainable livelihoods for our communities. However, there remains one major obstacle financial constraints. The growing burden of African public debt combined with illicit financial flows is reducing our room for maneuver. The additional needs for achieving the SDGs in Africa have been estimated at $1.6 trillion. At the same time, illicit capital flight is undermining our currency and our macroeconomic stability. Hence the need for urgent reform of the international financial architecture in order to guarantee that developing countries have fair and predictable access to concessional financing that is aligned with their national trajectories, including through a better channeling of special drawing rights, capitalization, and multilateral development banks, as well as countercyclical cash flows and a strengthened fight against illicit flows. Madam President, since I took up my post in my country, the DRC, I have pushed for a new dynamic in public affairs that include systematically the gender dimension at all levels to ensure heightened presence of women in decision-making bodies. For example, the percentage of women within the government has risen from 17% in 2019 to 32% in 2025. Madam President, as part of a strategic and multi-sectoral approach, that aims to mobilize the youth for national progress, my government has adopted a national youth policy.
